content: Gold salts refer to ionic chemical compounds of gold, though the term is somewhat misleading as many of these compounds are not true salts. These compounds are used in medicine under the terms chrysotherapy or aurotherapy. Their medical application began in 1935, primarily to reduce inflammation and slow disease progression in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis. Beyond medicine, gold compounds are also widely used in electroplating and as reagents in organic chemistry. Gold compounds accumulate gradually in the body and are used to reduce inflammation in diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, lupus erythematosus, membranous nephritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and, less commonly, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA). The exact mechanism of action remains under scientific investigation. It is believed that gold binds to albumin in the bloodstream, undergoing thiol exchange reactions, and is transported to the synovium. Once inside cells, gold is thought to exert anti-mitochondrial effects and induce apoptosis. However, the nonspecific absorption of gold compounds can lead to side effects, as they affect cells unrelated to the immune response in rheumatoid arthritis. Some researchers propose that gold compounds primarily suppress immune system components, such as phagocytes, leukocytes, and T-cells, thereby reducing inflammation and joint damage. Gold salts are rarely used in children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, as methotrexate is the preferred treatment. However, they may be considered for children with progressive polyarthritis unresponsive to other medications. This treatment is costly and requires frequent medical visits and laboratory monitoring. Gold drugs can be administered either orally or via intramuscular injection. Intramuscular injections are typically given weekly for three to five months before transitioning to less frequent doses. Auranofin, an oral gold compound, is marketed under the brand name Ridaura. Injectable forms include sodium aurothiomalate (Myocrisin in the UK, Aurolate or Myochrysine in the US) and aurothioglucose (Solganal in the US). Regular monitoring through urine and blood tests is necessary to detect potential kidney damage or other adverse effects. A 2005 review by Suarez-Almazor et al. found that intramuscular gold therapy reduces disease activity and joint inflammation, while oral gold compounds are less effective. Noticeable symptom improvement often requires three to six months of treatment. A 2002 study by Richards et al. highlighted neurological side effects of gold salts and suggested that gold might have therapeutic potential for neurological disorders. This research could expand the use of gold compounds beyond their current applications. Side effects of gold therapy can occur after significant accumulation of the compound in the body. Gold compounds take up to two months to reach a steady state and have a long half-life, with only 70% excreted within 10 days, increasing the risk of toxicity. Patients with pre-existing conditions, such as inflammatory bowel disease, skin rashes, or bone marrow depression, should weigh the benefits against the risks of gold toxicity. Oral gold compounds generally have fewer side effects than intramuscular injections. Common side effects of oral gold include decreased appetite, nausea, hair thinning, diarrhea, and issues affecting the skin, blood, kidneys, or lungs. Injectable gold can cause itchy skin rashes or mouth sores, with rare cases of kidney damage or blood cell suppression. Emerging research suggests potential new uses for gold salts. Boyd Haley has proposed their use in autism therapies. Gold salts are also being investigated as anti-cancer agents, particularly for their toxicity toward leukemia cells and effectiveness against cisplatin-resistant cancer cells. Additionally, gold salts combined with chloroquine show promise in treating resistant malaria strains. In Japan, gold thioglucose, used for rheumatoid arthritis, has been suggested as a potential treatment for bronchial asthma. Medically used gold salts include auranofin, aurothioglucose, disodium aurothiomalate, sodium aurothiosulfate, and sodium aurothiomalate. Industrially, potassium gold cyanide (KAu(CN)2), which contains 68.2% gold by weight, is used in electroplating but poses risks such as occupational contact eczema.
